transcript.content: Hi, welcome. What brings you in today?

Well… doctor, I came because I’ve been doing some odd things at church, and folks are starting to notice. It’s mostly around the potluck and helping set up. Like I’ll be standing there by the table with the serving spoon in my hand, held up like I’m about to scoop something, but then I just don’t move. I stay that way, and people are kind of looking at me, waiting.

And another thing is the napkins. I’ll take the same stack and fold them, then fold them again, and I know people are waiting on me or trying to get past, but I just keep doing it. It’s embarrassing, because I don’t mean to make trouble. I’ve gone to that church a long time, and I don’t want people thinking I’m being strange on purpose.
When you keep folding the napkins, do you feel driven to do it by a thought or urge that won’t leave you alone until you do it?

I don’t know if I’d call it an urge exactly, doctor. It’s not like I’m thinking, “I have to fold these or something bad will happen,” not in words like that. I just sort of… get caught in it. I’ll have the napkins in my hands, and I fold one side, then the other, and then I notice it’s not sitting right, or maybe I don’t even know what I notice, and I start again.

People will be moving around me, and I can tell I ought to stop, but it’s like my hands keep going before I really decide. I’m not sure if that’s an urge or just me getting stuck. I haven’t paid close enough attention to what’s in my mind right then, because mostly I’m embarrassed and trying to act normal.
When you were a child, did you often do repetitive things like rocking, flapping your hands, or lining objects up?

I’m not really sure, doctor. That’s going back a long ways for me. I don’t remember doing things like flapping my hands or rocking, not that I can clearly say. And lining things up… I don’t know. Children do little habits, you know, and my memory from then isn’t so sharp.

Nobody in my family ever made a point of telling me I did those things, at least not that I recall. If I did, it must not have stood out enough for folks to keep bringing it up. I remember ordinary things more than that, but I don’t want to say yes to something if I’m not sure.
When you get stuck holding the serving spoon, if someone gently moves your arm into a different position, does it tend to stay there?

I’m not sure about that exact part, doctor. I mean, nobody has really tried to move my arm like that, not in a way I can remember. What I do know is I’ll be standing there by the potluck table with the serving spoon held up, like I’m about to serve the food, and then I just… don’t go on with it. I sort of freeze there, and people are waiting.

It’s embarrassing, because I can tell it looks odd. And then with the napkins, I’ll get caught folding that same stack over and over while folks are trying to set things out or get past me. But as far as someone moving my arm and it staying where they put it, I can’t rightly say. I just know I get stuck in those positions or those little actions longer than I should.
When you are sitting still, do your hands ever shake on their own?

I don’t think so, doctor. Not that I’ve noticed, anyway. I mean, my hands aren’t as steady as when I was young, I suppose, but sitting still and them shaking all by themselves… I can’t say I’ve seen that.

Sometimes I look down at my hands if I’m holding something, because I get worried I’m doing something odd and people are noticing, but I don’t remember them trembling on their own while they’re just resting in my lap. If it happens, it must be small enough that I haven’t paid it much attention.
When you get caught folding the napkins, do unwanted thoughts keep popping into your mind that make it hard to stop?

I don’t know that I’d call them thoughts, doctor. Not like a certain thing popping in my head and telling me, “Fold it again,” or something like that. I haven’t noticed that.

It’s more like my hands just keep doing it, and I get sort of caught in the doing of it. I might know I should stop because people are waiting or the napkins are already folded enough, but it doesn’t feel like there’s some unwanted thought that keeps coming back. It’s just… I’m there, folding, and then I’m still folding, and it takes me a bit to come out of it.

I can feel embarrassed afterward, because I think, “Why did I keep doing that?” But at the time I’m not sure there’s much going through my mind that I can put words to.
When you get stuck like that, do you sometimes also become unable to speak?

Well… I don’t know if I’d say I can’t speak exactly, doctor. When it happens at church, like by the potluck table, I’ll just be standing there with the serving spoon lifted up, and folks are waiting for me to scoop something, and I don’t move on like I should. I’m aware enough to know it’s not right, but I feel sort of stuck there.

I might not answer right away if somebody says, “Are you all right?” but it isn’t always that my voice won’t work. It’s more like I’m caught in that odd moment, or with the napkins, I keep folding the same stack over and over, and people are trying to get around me. I get flustered and embarrassed, and sometimes I just don’t say much because I don’t know how to explain why I’m doing it.

So… maybe I get quiet, yes, but I’m not sure I become unable to speak. The main thing is I get stuck doing those strange things and can’t seem to move along like other people do.
Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?

I’m not sure, doctor. I don’t think I hear voices like someone standing in the room talking when nobody’s there, if that’s what you mean.

Sometimes I’ll think I heard something in the house, like a little sound or maybe someone calling from another room, and then I’ll listen and there’s nothing, but I don’t know if that’s just my ears or the house settling or me not paying attention. I live with a lot of quiet around me, and when it’s quiet, you can start noticing every little noise.

But voices… no, I can’t say that I’ve had a clear voice talking to me when no one was there. Not that I’ve noticed.
Do you ever find yourself automatically copying another person’s movements?

I don’t know that I copy other people’s movements, doctor. Not like if someone raises their hand and then I raise mine right after, or anything like that. I haven’t noticed that.

What I do notice, and it’s the reason I came in, is more that I get caught doing odd things myself. Like at church, by the potluck table, I’ll be holding the serving spoon up and just sort of stay there, not moving on, even though people are waiting. Or I’ll be folding the same stack of napkins over and over, and I know afterward it must have looked strange, because folks are trying to get past me or waiting for me to finish.

It’s embarrassing, because I don’t mean to make a scene. I’m not trying to imitate anybody. I just get stuck in what I’m doing, and then it takes me a while to come out of it.
Have you noticed that your walking has become shuffling?

I don’t know about shuffling, doctor. I haven’t really paid close attention to my walking like that. What brought me in is more those odd moments at church, where I get stuck doing something and people notice.

Like I’ll be at the potluck table with the serving spoon raised up, and instead of just scooping and moving along, I sort of stand there holding it. Or I’ll keep folding the same napkins over and over while folks are waiting on me, and then I feel embarrassed because I know it must look strange. But as far as my feet shuffling when I walk, I can’t really say I’ve noticed that.
Since you were young, have you usually found it hard to understand other people socially, like knowing how to join conversations or read what others mean from their facial expressions?

I’m not really sure, doctor. Since I was young… that’s a long time ago now, and I don’t know that I ever thought about it in that kind of way.

I wasn’t someone who studied people’s faces or conversations like that. I mean, I knew when somebody was mad if they were scolding me, or if people were laughing, I could tell that. But whether I had a special hard time joining in or reading expressions, I can’t really say. I don’t remember anyone telling me that was a problem when I was little.

I’ve always been more on the quiet side, I suppose, and I didn’t have a lot of schooling, so sometimes in groups I’d just listen more than talk. But I don’t know if that’s the same thing you mean. I wouldn’t want to say yes to something if I’m not sure.
Do you believe anyone is trying to harm you or control you?

I don’t know, doctor. I can’t say that I believe somebody is trying to harm me or control me, not in a clear way like that.

Sometimes I worry what people think of me, especially if I’ve acted odd or if I’ve held people up, but that’s more embarrassment, I think. I don’t have a name of a person, or a group, or anything like that that I think is after me. And I don’t feel like somebody is making me do things from the outside, if that’s what you mean by control.

I just… I’m not sure how to answer it beyond that. I don’t think anyone is out to hurt me.
Have you been diagnosed with any brain or nerve illness, such as Parkinson’s disease?

No, not that I know of, doctor. Nobody has told me I have Parkinson’s disease or any kind of brain or nerve illness.

I mean, I’ve seen doctors over the years for ordinary things, but I don’t remember anyone saying anything like that to me. If they did, I think I would remember, because that sounds like something serious. So as far as I know, no.
Did these getting-stuck episodes begin after a medical illness or injury?

I’m not really sure, doctor. I don’t remember it starting after some big illness or injury, no. I mean, I’ve had ordinary times of being unwell like anyone my age, but I can’t point to a fall, or an accident, or being in the hospital, or something like that and say, “That’s when it began.”

The getting stuck… it’s hard for me to place it neatly. It didn’t feel like there was one clear before-and-after moment, at least not that I can recall. If there was, nobody explained it to me that way, and I don’t have that kind of memory of it beginning right after something medical happened.
When you get stuck in a position, if someone gently moves your arm or hand, does it stay in the new position?

I’m not sure about the arm or hand staying if someone moves it, doctor. I don’t really remember people trying to move me like that, at least not in a way I can answer properly.

What made me come in is more that I get caught doing odd things at church. Like at the potluck table, I’ll be standing there with the serving spoon held up, just not moving along, and people are waiting, and I don’t seem to get myself started again right away. Or I’ll be folding the same little stack of napkins over and over, like I’m supposed to be helping, but I’m just repeating it while folks are trying to get past me.

It’s embarrassing, because church is where everybody knows you, and I don’t mean to hold anyone up or act strange. But about whether my hand would stay if somebody moved it… I just don’t know.
Have you found yourself talking much less than you used to?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed that, doctor. I mean, I still talk when people talk to me, and if I’m comfortable with someone I can go on for a while, as you can probably tell.

Maybe there are times I’m quieter, but I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly found myself talking much less than I used to. It’s hard for me to judge, because some days I don’t have much to say, and other days I’ll talk about little details and then realize I’ve been talking too long. So… no, not in a way I could point to for sure.
Do you feel that your movements in general have become slower than they used to be?

Slower in general… I don’t know if I would say it that way exactly, doctor. I’m not walking around thinking, “Oh, I’m slower than I used to be,” not all the time.

What I notice more is these odd moments, especially at church, where I just sort of stop or keep doing something that doesn’t make sense. Like I came in because I’ll be at the potluck table and I’ll be holding the serving spoon up, just standing there, and people are trying to get their food and I’m not moving along like I should. Or I’ll get stuck folding the same little stack of napkins over and over, and folks are waiting on me or needing the space.

So maybe it looks slow to other people, I don’t know. To me it feels more like I get caught, or I don’t shift to the next thing right when I’m supposed to. It’s embarrassing, because I’m not trying to be difficult or hold anybody up.
When you try to stop folding the napkins, do you start to feel anxious?

I’m not really sure it’s anxiety, doctor. I don’t always notice a feeling like panic or being scared when I try to stop. Sometimes I’m more just aware that I ought to stop, because somebody needs the napkins or I can see people moving around me, and then I feel embarrassed or flustered because I’m still doing it.

But if you mean do I feel nervous inside, like my heart racing or worrying something bad will happen if I stop, I don’t know that I can say that. It’s more like I get caught in the doing of it, and then when I realize people are noticing, that’s when I feel uncomfortable.
Has anyone ever moved your arm or hand while you were stuck, and then it stayed in that new position for a while?

I don’t know that anyone has actually moved my arm or hand like that, doctor. I can’t say yes to that part.

What happens is more that I get stuck doing the odd thing myself. Like at church, by the potluck table, I’ll be holding the serving spoon up and just not moving along, even though people are waiting and needing to get to the food. Or with the napkins, I’ll keep folding the same little stack over and over, and I know it doesn’t make much sense, but I’m still doing it.

If someone has touched my arm to get my attention, I don’t remember it staying where they put it or anything like that. It’s more me getting caught in the action, if that makes sense.
When you freeze like that, has anyone ever gently repositioned your arm and then it stayed that way for a while?

I don’t think anybody has repositioned my arm like that, doctor—not where they put it somewhere and then it stayed there. What I keep trying to explain is more that I get stuck in what I’m already doing.

Like at church, I’ll be by the potluck table with the serving spoon, and I’ll just be standing there holding it up, not moving along, while people are waiting behind me. Or I’ll be folding the same little stack of napkins again and again, and folks need them or need the space, and I know I ought to stop but I just keep at it for a bit.

So no, I don’t remember someone gently moving my arm and it staying there. It’s more those odd moments where I’m doing something that doesn’t make sense and I don’t shift out of it right away.
